You will start with the basis, while you will see that documentation is big too. Using Vim can speed up our work. When opening a new file with Vim , type i to start writting and use ESC keyboard to go back to Normal Mode . When you type i you are using Vim in Insert Mode . In Normal Mode you can select text areas, using v to select one or more characters, or the sequence Shift+v to select one or more lines, and you enter the Visual Mode . Enter the command : to enter the Command Mode and by using the TAB key of your keyboard, explore all available commands. Always use :help command . Type :w to save changes and :close to close a file or use :q to leave editor. You can use sequences of commands , like for example: :waq! . This command save by the option :w , :a means all files in session , and :q is to quit and leave editor. Sometimes we can open a Terminal with :terminal or a File Explorer with :Sexplorer inside Vim . By using :! we force leaving Vim editor. Use u to undo changes or :q! to exit Vim without saving changes. Today I figure out that I wish to add a new HTML class into all posts of this blog that use the same CSS configurations. I just type vim * into the docs/ directory and all posts where there, in one single page. Then you ask: how can the editor open more than 300 files and we only see one? And the answer is buffers . Use the command :buffers or :ls to list all files in buffers. For example :buffer 69 or the shortcut :b 69 will open the 69 file in buffer. You can use :bnext or bpreviews to jump between open files . Use / in Normal Mode to find some text and use :%s/text-to-modify/modified-text/ to change one single line or :%s/text-to-modify/modified-text/g to change all lines with the same text You wish to change. Use n to jump to the next text or Shift+n to jump to the previous one. To record a macro you need to press q in Normal Mode , to start and create the sequence you need to do in many files, and press q to stop recording. Use the . to repeat the last changes into all other files. I could create a macro to apply the same commands (select and add new content) within all files. For this example we would do something like: q to start recording the macro , hit ESC key to enter Normal Mode , type / to search the text I wish to change, /text and hit enter , then I access the Command Mode and type :%s/text/newText/g and hit Enter Key to change, next hit ESC key to go back to Normal Mode and finally hit q to stop recording the macro . You can easly work in several files in the same "Window" using the :vsplit option to open new files in a vertical direction and :split in a horizontal one. Use the sequnce Ctrl+w+w to jump between splits. You can use tabs too if you prefer instead but at the end, you cannot have 300 tabs open, while you can have them in memory ( buffers ). Since in this specific case we only add content to some HTML class , in fact I use this solution to make all changes in less than 3 seconds and without opening any file on any text editor. I think the number of visits continue to grow, depending on the days, mostly in the middle of the week, not in the weeken. Strange, but is what the numbers say. Singapore continue to explore the videos (is anyone there who understand Portuguese?) Hong Kong continue to explore all other domains. Canada too, Portugal too. I think people didn’t register into Github, to share some comments with me, so… I continue to be the Monkey who doesn’t listen, while I can read but no one write me a bit. Enjoy the Show! :D What the pattern suggests A real audience has a rhythm. People read during the week, at work or between two tasks, and they disappear on the weekend because the weekend belongs to something else. A machine does not care about Saturdays, although a lot of automated traffic slows down when the offices that host it are closed. So a curve that falls on Saturday can mean readers, and it can also mean crawlers running on company infrastructure. I cannot separate the two with the summary alone, and that uncertainty is the honest state of anyone who looks at a dashboard of a small site. The geography of a small blog Singapore looking at the videos, Hong Kong looking at everything, Canada, Portugal, the United States, Germany, Turkey, India, Brazil. A list like that says more about the network than about the audience. Big hosting providers sit in a few countries, and their addresses make the map look global even when the visitor is one room away. And yet the question about Portuguese remains. Somebody in Singapore is opening pages in a language that is not the language of the country, which is either a very patient reader or a very confused proxy. The silence of the reader Nobody writes. Not because nobody reads, but because writing costs something and reading does not. To leave a comment you need an account, and to create an account you need a reason, and a reason is exactly what a stranger does not have. So I keep writing and I keep reading the silence, which is the most common form of feedback on the Internet. The Monkey who doesn't listen is also the Monkey who doesn't demand. Enjoy the Show. :D
vontadeDivina: Assuntos do Céu, Gestão da Terra Vontade Divina Existe uma teologia inteira, em cada credo, dedicada a explicar porque é que alguém dorme no chão frio. Não é por falta de tempo: dois mil, quatro mil anos de reflexão, concílios, bibliotecas e teólogos oficiais, e a resposta final que chega à calçada é sempre a mesma, entregue com a compostura de quem despede um hóspede chato: é vontade divina . A pessoa está na rua porque o Céu assim o quis. E a vontade divina é uma solução administrativa admirável: nunca pediu nada a ninguém, nunca assinou uma petição , nunca apareceu numa manifestação , e por isso nunca atrasou o jantar de ninguém. Enquanto isso, do lado de lá do vidro da janela quente, há gente sem teto , sem toalha, sem sabonete, sem moeda no bolso, sem voto que mude qualquer coisa, sem porta onde pôr uma chave, a envelhecer em público sobre o betão. E há também gente voluptuosamente dentro de casa, com horários litúrgicos cheios: dia de oração, dia de jejum, dia de procissão, dia de vigília, dia de festa, dia de missa, dia de recolhimento. O calendário sacro , em cada confissão, tem espaço para tudo. Menos para isso. O plano de habitação social do Altíssimo Observe-se a grandiosidade da engenharia divina: criou-se o vasto universo, as marés, as ondas, as solas dos pés e os preços dos telhados, e deliberadamente não se criou habitação social . Que descuido genial, sem dúvida: se nem o dono da casa arranjou casa, quem sou eu, ser humano provincial, para discordar do proprietário? É uma escola de obediência. Não repara esta escola na jurisdição da conveniência: nenhum credo, sem excepção nenhum, conseguiu até hoje escrever nos seus estatutos a linha simples "e aos sábados, pelas pessoas sem casa, vamos todos à praça" . Dois mil anos de patentes, sinodais, assembleias, concílios e orações, e a linha mais simples da moral prática continua em branco. Dizem que a fé move montanhas. Obra magnífica, sem dúvida. Só que a montanha ninguém pediu. O que estava em cima da mesa era um pedido infinitamente mais modesto: que a fé movesse uma pessoa três ruas até à Câmara Municipal num sábado às três da tarde, de sapatos calçados, para exigir que ninguém durma no frio. Resultado laboratorial: a montanha continua no seu lugar e o crente também. Conclui-se que sempre foi mais fácil mover pedras mudas, incapazes de queixar-se e de informar, do que levar um adulto de apartamento aquecido a dar dois passos de solidariedade em direção a alguém que pode olhá-lo nos olhos. O jejum é fácil quando se conta com o jantar Repare-se na dedicação técnica dos fiéis quando o cliente da devoção é a própria alma. Levantam-se de madrugada. Seguem jejuns , novenas , peregrinações, vigílias , retiros, litanias, escalas. Regulam-se as dobras do hábito da espiritualidade como quem ajusta um relógio suíço . Toda uma logística, com cartazes, horários, folhetos e sistemas de notificações, para certificar a ocupação sagrada do dia. E quando essa mesma agenda cheia atravessa uma praça onde se discute uma manta para quem dorme ao frio, o fiel traduz o dilema instantaneamente. Escolhe a oração, e não é mistério: a oração é barata, é silenciosa, não exige sapatos, não molha, não tem hora marcada, e atribui o mérito a uma terceira pessoa celestial que, ao fim de tantos séculos, ainda não pôs os pés em nenhum abrigo para cortar as fitas. "Vou rezar por eles." A frase com que tanta gente leva, lavada, seca e dobrada , uma consciência intacta. O currículo espiritual não pede anexos. O mérito da oração nunca é auditado. Pergunte-se ao fiel o que fez pelas pessoas sem teto: "orei por elas", e espera-se, por hábito, um aplauso. Numa entrevista de emprego, quem escrevesse no currículo "enviei bons pensamentos ao departamento de vendas durante oito anos" seria escoltado para a porta por fraude documental. Na contabilidade espiritual, pelo contrário, o documento é aceito sem recibo, sem verificação, sem data de validade. Milhares de horas de oração por pessoas concretas produzem, em consonância com a perfeição do método, exactamente zero manta, zero duche, zero cama, zero tigela de sopa. Arquiva-se a folha, e a folha fica limpa. As pessoas ficam na chuva . Quatrocentos metros de penitência impossível Há quem atravesse continentes para tocar uma relíquia . Filas de comboios, peregrinações de autocarro, multidões cantando com os pés em feridas, hora que ninguém reclama, dinheiro que ninguém conta. O mesmo crente que assim se desloca ombro a ombro com a multidão para tocar um osso antigo, não atravessa os quatrocentos metros do seu bairro até à Câmara Municipal para uma manifestação pelas pessoas sem casa. Não é falta de força, e muito pouco é geografia: é contrato. A relíquia devolve mérito, actualiza a poupança eterna , tem carimbo . A praça devolve apenas um incómodo civil: o aviso de que as decisões políticas pertencem, também, à consciência de quem dorme aquecido. E essa conta já está paga, dizem, por um intermediário muito mais alto , com uma moratória assinada lá atrás, há dois mil anos. Assim acontece que as manifestações pelas pessoas sem teto têm uma demografia cristalina : os próprios sem teto, que não têm alternativa, dois ou três militantes de sempre, e ninguém mais. Em quantidade, os crentes são legião, certamente, mas ausentam-se com elegância: silenciosa, respeitosa, litúrgica. A fertilidade dos altares contrasta com o deserto da praça. Onde há pão abençoado , há multidão auditada até à última cadeira. Onde há exigência de pão simplesmente abençoado pela mão humana, há vento. Os sem-deus também têm lugares marcados E agora, com a mesma tesoura, a outra equipa: os que ostentam não ter credo nenhum . Dispõem de factos , gráficos , tabelas , citações da ciência. Explicam, com razão ilustrada, que o céu não constrói paredes, que a matéria é matéria e que a ordem social se decide aqui em baixo. Perfeito. E depois? Isto é a parte divertida: também não vão às manifestações. Têm, contudo, um hobby superior e muito gratificante: discordar . Discorda-se do Eterno em textos compridos, no sofá, com um café e dois comentários compridos. Prova-se que a religião falhou, prova-se que o Estado falhou, prova-se que tudo falhou, e remata-se a obra com a prova final e mais sólida de todas: a prova de que agora não é o momento. Os seus ritos de devoção incluem partilhar indignação, reagir com fúria e escolher a manta, não da cama, mas da escada de serviço. Ir é grátis, não há excomunhão , não há direcção espiritual a pedir perdão por ter dado dois passos. E mesmo assim, a cadência é igual: o sofá . A solidariedade adiada tem, hoje, no Ocidente aquecido, um patrono universal: a vontade própria. Uns dizem que foi Deus ; outros dizem que foi o trânsito . O patrono varia, o produto é o mesmo: ausência com justificação. A consciência folgada tem, como se vê, um fabricante por credo. Ligam um interruptor cada manhã e a culpa fica lá fora, a tremer com a chuva. Outras praças, outra inércia E o caso não é o das pessoas sem casa. Não percam de vista o resto do programa: salários que não chegam ao fim do mês, a habitação que custa o salário de uma vida, a saúde que demora, a educação que endivida, as guerras que recebem bombas contratadas a prazo. Convoca-se a praça para exigir decisões que afectam a vida dos cidadãos, e a praça responde com o mesmo vazio testemunhal. Arquitectura da ausência, em duas variantes eternas: o crente fica em casa porque às decisões políticas preside César , e o César, dizem as escrituras, inflaciona por conta própria; o sem-deus fica em casa porque as manifestações não valem nada, as coalizões são vendidas pelo sistema, e a inutilidade é um argumento magnífico, cómodo, nunca testado experimentalmente por quem o profere. Testá-lo exigiria ir. Ir é o único passo que as duas escatologias, a do céu e a do sofá, nunca coordenaram. Há uma hipótese antiquíssima que ninguém teve coragem de dissolver: talvez o poder político seja exactamente proporcional ao número de pessoas dispostas a sair de casa por quem não tem casa. Um só indivíduo na praça é um anónimo; mil é uma exigência; mil crentes e mil sem-deus juntos, na mesma calçada , é uma decisão. Mas exigir é desconfortável, e a humanidade tem feito um investimento magnífico em conforto: construiu-se a mais sofisticada infra-estrutura de excusas da história, com teologia de um lado, sociologia do outro, e no meio de tudo, as pessoas que dormem no chão como nunca dormiram os que discutem sobre elas. Sem excepções Que ninguém venha dizer "mas há de sempre os que ajudam". Ajudar é o que as pessoas fazem, não o que os credos ensinam; e aqui não se fala de excepções, fala-se da regra: todas as comunidades de fé , todas, e todas as de não-fé. Todos os credos, no plural e sem excepção, têm templos cheios e praças vazias . Todas as tradições têm um método próprio de escrever a palavra amanhã . Todo o crente reza pelo que dorme na chuva e volta a dormir na cama aquecida. Todo o sem-deus analisa o que dorme na chuva e volta a dormir na cama aquecida também. O discurso muda. A cama , não. Nem os jubileus, nem os congressos de milhares, nem as assembleias onde o povo eleito se abençoa mutuamente por horas, decidem nunca marchar. O calendário universal tem espaço, e é justo reconhecê-lo, para peregrinações internacionais por motivos devocionais de toda a espécie. Assinala o Dia da Criação. Assinala as Jornadas da Juventude , com multidões imensas a dormir no chão duro, de bom grado, porque é de fé. É a ironia mais brutal da história: milhares de jovens dormem no chão em nome de Deus por vontade própria , e não um único é enviado com o mesmo alistamento até à praça em nome dos que dormem no chão por falta de vontade humana . warManifesto: The Logic of Contained War: Why Wars Must Be Fought in a Dedicated Zone, By Soldiers Only, With Superiors First A Rational, Logical, Moral, Legal, Economic, Ecological and Satirical Treatise in Twenty-Three Chapters. Thesis: If war is to exist at all in a rational civilization, then (1) it must take place in a dedicated zone containing no other living beings who are not consenting soldiers, and (2) the so-called “superiors” — generals, ministers, presidents, war councils, arms executives who declare and profit from war — must by logic be the first bodies in that zone. Since samurai masters went first while students were forbidden to precede them, modern rank must be earned the same way: superiority shall be proven by the ability to outrun bullets and missiles. If you cannot dodge a missile, you are not superior. You are merely distant. 1. Introduction: Reason Against Organized Madness Let us begin with a proposition so simple that only a general staff could misunderstand it: if two groups of human beings decide that they must kill each other to resolve a disagreement, there is no rational justification for involving a third group that did not agree to be killed. This is not pacifism. This text is not written by a pacifist, nor for pacifists alone. It is written from the coldest possible rationality, the kind that engineers use when they refuse to build a bridge that will fall, that doctors use when they refuse to prescribe poison as medicine, that logicians use when they refuse to accept that A and not-A are both true. War, as currently practiced, is illogical. Not merely immoral — illogical. It claims to be a contest between armed forces, a test of will between states, a defense of values by soldiers, and then it proceeds to kill precisely those who are not armed, not contesting, not willing, and not responsible: infants in maternity wards, grandmothers in kitchens, farmers in fields, schoolchildren on buses, dogs, cats, donkeys, forests, coral reefs, and entire ecosystems that never signed any enlistment form. Consider the logic of any other dangerous human activity. If two boxers wish to fight, we do not permit them to punch spectators on the way to the ring and call it collateral damage. We build a ring. We put only the two consenting fighters inside it. We surround it with ropes. We appoint a referee. We forbid weapons beyond padded gloves. We stop the fight when one cannot continue. We do not bomb the audience because one boxer is hiding behind them. If we did, we would call it murder and imprison the boxer, the coach, and the promoter. Why, then, when the scale grows from two men to two armies, does logic invert? Why does mass murder become strategy, and the slaughter of uninvolved life become an unfortunate but acceptable externality? The answer is not logic. The answer is power protecting itself from logic. This treatise proposes a restoration of logic in two moves. First move: spatial and ontological containment. All war must occur in a Dedicated Zone, a legally delimited, ecologically sterilized in the sense of no non-combatant life, geographically isolated arena containing only consenting soldiers and their equipment. No cities, no villages, no hospitals, no schools, no farms, no forests with fauna, no seas with marine life, no skies with migratory birds. Only soldiers, only weapons they carry, only ground designated for destruction. Second move: hierarchical inversion corrected. Those who order war, who declare themselves superior in rank, wisdom, patriotism, or strategic genius, must be physically first in that zone. Not symbolically first, not first in a televised speech, but first in space and time: first boots on the designated ground, first bodies exposed to the fire they ordered. For superiority, if the word means anything, must mean superior exposure to risk, superior willingness to bear the consequence, superior proof by presence. Otherwise superiority means only superior distance from consequence, which is not superiority but parasitism. These two principles will be defended here not by sentiment but by rational argument: moral philosophy, law, economics, ecology, game theory, organizational psychology, and history. And then, because pure logic is sometimes too polite to wound vanity, we will add satire, after the manner of Juvenal and Swift: if modern superiors insist they are superior while remaining in bunkers, we shall take them at their word and test that superiority empirically. Samurai masters led the charge while students were forbidden to go before them. Therefore let our generals, ministers, and war profiteers prove rank by outrunning bullets and missiles. If they are truly superior beings, this should be trivial. If they cannot, let rank be reassigned to those who can, namely, in practice, no one — which is precisely the point, and why contained war with superiors first would make war nearly disappear. A note on method: rationality here means the systematic pursuit of non-contradiction, universality, and proportionality. A rational rule is one that can be stated without contradiction, applied universally without self-exemption, and proportioned to its stated end. Current war fails all three tests. It contradicts its own justification (defending life by destroying uninvolved life), it exempts its authors (those who decide do not die), and it is wildly disproportionate (to kill one combatant, kill a hundred civilians and poison a province for decades). Contained war with superiors first passes all three: it kills only those who consented to kill, it exposes deciders first, and it limits destruction to a place chosen for that purpose. Whether you love your country or despise all armies, logic compels the same conclusion. The chapters that follow build this case step by step. We will examine consent, ecology, economy, law, philosophy, psychology, technology, logistics, and treaty drafting. We will answer every serious objection: that war cannot be contained, that superiors are too valuable to risk, that deterrence requires threatening civilians, that history proves total war inevitable. Each objection will be shown to be either false, cowardly, or self-refuting. And interwoven throughout, we will return to the central joke that is not a joke: if you are superior, go first. Dodge the missile. Show us. 2. First Axiom: Killing Without Consent Is Murder, Even in Uniform The foundation of all criminal law in every rational society is the distinction between killing with justification and killing without it. Self-defense against an immediate lethal attacker is justified because the attacker, by attacking, consented to the risk of defensive force. Dueling, boxing, and soldiering are historically treated as special cases where mutual consent to lethal risk transforms what would otherwise be murder into something else — combat. The crucial element is mutuality of consent among participants. Remove that, and you revert to murder. A civilian child in a besieged city has not consented to be bombed. A farmer has not consented to have his field mined. A nurse has not consented to have her hospital struck because an enemy sniper may be on its roof. A stray dog has not consented to anything at all, lacking the conceptual apparatus for consent, and therefore must be treated under the same protective principle we apply to infants and the mentally incapacitated: the inability to consent means we may not presume it. To kill them in order to kill soldiers is to use them as means, in Kantian terms, as mere instruments for military ends. It violates the categorical imperative in the most literal way: treat humanity never merely as a means but always as an end. A bomb dropped on a market to kill two insurgents treats fifty shoppers as means — as acceptable friction on the way to a military end. No rational ethics can survive that permission, because once you permit using the non-consenting as means for the sake of the consenting combatants’ goals, you have permitted everything: torture, hostage-taking, genocide, all justified as friction. The standard rebuttal — military necessity, proportionality, distinction as currently interpreted — is logic laundered through euphemism. International humanitarian law already recognizes the principle but enforces it weakly: it forbids deliberate targeting of civilians yet tolerates “incidental” killing if “proportionate” to military advantage. This is a loophole large enough to fly a bomber through. Who measures proportionality? The bomber. Who defines military advantage? The bomber’s superior, sitting far away. Who counts the dead? Often no one, or the bomber’s own press office. A rational system cannot leave the murder / not-murder distinction to the murderer’s discretion. It must be structural, not discretionary. Structure means space: if non-consenters are not in the space where killing happens, they cannot be incidentally killed. The Dedicated Zone is therefore not a utopian luxury; it is the only physical implementation of the consent principle that does not rely on the goodwill of killers in the heat of killing. Consider an analogy from medicine. Surgeons consent to bloody work; patients consent to be cut open for cure. We do not therefore permit surgeons to operate in a crowded subway car with a scalpel, nicking bystanders as collateral incisions. We require an operating theater: sterilized, restricted, consented. War claims to be surgery on the body politic — excising aggression, removing tyranny. Even if we grant the metaphor, surgery requires a theater. Open war in inhabited areas is surgery in a subway car. It is malpractice by design. From this axiom flows a corollary that will recur: any military doctrine that presupposes the presence of civilians as cover, shield, deterrent, or pressure point is inherently criminal, regardless of which side employs it. If an army hides among civilians, it violates consent. If the opposing army then bombs those civilians to get at that army, it also violates consent, and two violations do not make a justification. The rational solution is not to debate which violator is worse but to remove the condition that makes the debate possible: no war where civilians live. Period. If you cannot fight without endangering non-consenters, you cannot rationally claim to fight justly. You must either not fight, or move the fight. 3. A Brief History of Contained Violence: From Duels to Demilitarized Zones Humanity has always known that violence must be contained to remain intelligible. The earliest forms of organized combat were bounded. Tribal battles were often fought at agreed places and times, with non-combatants excluded. The Iliad, for all its gore, describes champions meeting between armies, and armies pausing to collect their dead. Medieval judicial duels, however barbaric, understood consent and place: a field, witnesses, equal arms. Tournaments confined knightly violence to lists. Even the duel of honor in early modern Europe — two men, pistols, dawn, seconds — was an attempt, however flawed, to prevent feuds from spilling into families and streets. The logic was always the same: if men must kill, let only those men be at risk, elsewhere. The modern state broke this wisdom by inventing total war. The Napoleonic levée en masse, Sherman’s march, the blockade of Germany in World War I, Guernica, Hamburg, Dresden, Hiroshima — each step normalized the idea that the enemy is not the enemy army but the enemy society. Strategic bombing theory explicitly argued that breaking civilian morale wins wars faster than defeating armies. Nuclear deterrence completed the inversion: peace maintained by threatening to murder millions of non-consenters in minutes. This is historically anomalous and rationally indefensible, yet it is presented as realism. Realism, in this usage, means resigned acceptance of the most unrealistic proposition of all: that threatening to destroy the world keeps the world safe. But counter-examples prove containment is possible when will exists. The Antarctic Treaty demilitarized an entire continent. The Outer Space Treaty forbids weapons of mass destruction in space. Boxing commissions, however corrupt, still enforce rings and weight classes. The Olympics replaced war with sport in a dedicated zone — stadium — with strict exclusion of non-athletes from the field. Even within war, the concept of hospital ships, prisoner-of-war camps, and demilitarized zones shows that armies can, when ordered, respect spatial distinctions. If we can mark a hospital with a red cross and (mostly) not bomb it, we can mark a war zone with a black border and only bomb inside it. The technical capacity is not lacking; the moral will of superiors is lacking, because open war externalizes cost onto civilians while contained war would internalize cost onto soldiers and especially onto superiors. History also gives us the precedent for superiors first. Alexander fought in the front rank and was wounded multiple times. Leonidas died with his 300. Medieval kings who lost battles often lost their lives or crowns on the field — Richard III died at Bosworth, Harold at Hastings. Samurai daimyo and their senior retainers led charges; to send ashigaru peasants forward while hiding was dishonor punishable by loss of status. The shift to distant command came with artillery range, telegraph, and then radio, which allowed generals to claim credit without sharing risk. World War I crystallized the obscenity: generals in châteaux ordering millions into machine-gun fire, then awarding themselves medals. The rest of the twentieth century perfected it: air-conditioned command centers, video feeds, press briefings. Contained war with superiors first is therefore not innovation but restoration — a return to the older, more logical equation where authority equals exposure. 4. The Dedicated Zone: Definition, Logic, and Necessity Principle 1 — The Containment Principle: No act of war is legitimate outside a previously delimited Dedicated War Zone (DWZ) containing zero non-consenting living beings. Any killing outside the DWZ is murder, any destruction outside is vandalism, regardless of uniform, flag, or order. Define the Dedicated War Zone as follows: a tract of land, sea platform, or combined area, no smaller than necessary for maneuver and no larger than necessary to avoid waste, selected precisely because it contains no permanent civilian habitation, no agriculture for civilian use, no hospitals or schools, no religious sites in use, no critical infrastructure for non-combatants, and no resident non-human animal populations beyond transient microbes and, after clearance, zero vertebrates. It is surveyed, fenced in legal terms by treaty and in physical terms by sensors, walls, and patrols, evacuated, monitored by neutral observers, and designated as the sole locus where lethal force between belligerents is permitted. Entry is by enlistment and informed consent only. Exit for civilians is guaranteed before hostilities; entry for journalists is restricted to remote observation; entry for wildlife is prevented by barriers and deterrents. The logic is syllogistic. Major premise: legitimate lethal force requires consent of those at risk or their immediate aggression. Minor premise: outside a dedicated zone, those at risk have neither consented nor aggressed. Conclusion: lethal force outside is illegitimate. This is as tight as logic gets. To deny the conclusion you must deny a premise, which means asserting either that consent does not matter (pure tyranny) or that civilians in war areas have somehow consented by merely living there (victim-blaming metaphysics). Both denials collapse under universalization: if consent does not matter, then your own civilians may be killed without wrong; if living somewhere equals consent to be bombed, then living in a capital that orders war equals consent to be assassinated — a conclusion superiors will never accept for themselves, proving they do not believe their own premise. Necessity follows from the failure of all milder alternatives. Rules of engagement, precision weapons, and proportionality reviews have not prevented civilian death; they have merely bureaucratized it. The statistics are monotonous across decades: in modern wars, civilian deaths equal or exceed military deaths, often by multiples. Precision does not solve presence. A precise bomb in a crowded street still kills the street. The only variable that reliably reduces civilian casualties to zero is absence — the absence of civilians from the blast radius. Since we cannot make weapons non-lethal to bystanders, we must make bystanders absent from weapons. The zone does that structurally. It replaces discretion (“try not to hit civilians”) with impossibility (“there are no civilians to hit”). Engineers prefer impossibility over exhortation; so should moralists. Objections about fluid warfare — insurgency, terrorism, cyber — will be addressed fully in Chapter 22, but note here that the zone does not excuse non-state actors from containment; it obliges states to refuse to wage open war even against open attackers, and instead to draw, lure, compel, or require combat in the zone through a combination of defensive fortification of civilian areas, evacuation, and refusal to deploy heavy weapons outside the zone. If an attacker refuses the zone and attacks civilians, that attacker is by definition a murderer, not a warrior, and must be pursued by policing, not by counter-murder. The state that responds to terrorism by terror-bombing neighborhoods has abandoned logic for mimicry. Finally, the zone restores the meaning of victory. In open war, victory is ambiguous: did you defeat the army or merely exhaust the civilian population? In contained war, victory is crisp: the force that can no longer field consenting soldiers in the zone loses. No need to starve cities, no need to break morale, no need to count corpses of children as progress. War becomes what it pretends to be — a contest of soldiers — and therefore reveals its own futility faster, because without civilian suffering to exploit, the only thing consumed is the war machine itself. 5. No Other Living Beings: Children, Civilians, Animals, Forests, and Seas The phrase “without other living beings that are not soldiers” must be taken literally and expanded ecologically. Modern war does not only kill humans who did not consent; it kills donkeys, dogs, cats, cattle, birds, fish, bees, forests, mangroves, and microbial balances that sustain life. Depleted uranium, oil fires, sonar blasts, drift nets of naval war, defoliants — the casualties include entire food webs. A rational ethic cannot restrict moral considerability to uniformed humans while ignoring sentient non-humans and life-support systems, because destroying those systems destroys the very humans war claims to defend, just more slowly. Consider the cow. She does not vote, does not enlist, does not hate the enemy. Yet in every rural war she is shot for sport, blown up by mines, starved when fields burn, or slaughtered for logistics. Consider the dog in a bombed suburb, deafened, buried, starving beside its dead owner. Consider the whale deafened by naval sonar, beaching itself. Consider the olive grove, a century old, uprooted for a berm. None consented. None can be compensated with medals or pensions. Their suffering is pure externality, invisible in strategic briefings. A dedicated zone with no other living beings means, in implementation: prior ecological survey, relocation of livestock and pets, wildlife corridors closed during conflict, sonic and chemical exclusion, minefields mapped and only inside, no use of rivers that flow to civilian agriculture, no atmospheric releases that drift to inhabited areas, no naval battles in breeding grounds. It means war must be biologically sterile outside its participants — as sterile as an operating theater. Is this demanding? Ye

xtermHero: ↶ Home Field Manual XTH-2 · nothing to hero, one window at a time xterm — From Nothing to Hero The terminal that is already there before you pick an emulator. It has no opinions, no plugins and no settings UI — but it has menus hidden behind mouse chords, a resource database, a 256-colour palette and a translation system for keys. Everything in one page. menus · resources · colors · fonts · scrollback vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies titles get hijacked, politely, on demand 01 From nothing xterm is the X Window System's own terminal emulator — the original one, shipped with X itself since the 1980s and still maintained. That placement is its whole personality: It is always there. Install X on BSD or Linux and xterm appears with it. When your fancy emulator breaks, when you are setting up a new window manager, when you ssh into a machine with no dotfiles — it is the window you open next. It does not fight. No shells inside the emulator, no plugin sandboxes, no theme marketplace. Features are negotiated with the X server like it is 1985, which means they are all still documented. It is the reference. Ctrl-click menus, clipboard semantics, mouse support, 256 colours — if a modern emulator implements something differently, xterm's way is what the man page compares against first. On most systems it comes as a standalone package ( x11/xterm on BSD, xterm everywhere else), which drags in one small friend worth celebrating later: resize(1) . Note: “hero” here means: you can configure xterm without a drinking problem, name menus by their chords, and fix five classic puzzles (frozen screen, ghost Alt , vanished titles, stale size after split, missing clipboard bridge). Those five, named and fixed in a minute — that is the hero part. 02 First launch that sticks From an X session (cwm, twm, anything with a launcher), the zeroth xterm is one command: $ xterm & And the four flags that cover every practical first launch: $ xterm -ls # login shell, reads .profile like a console $ xterm -e htop # run a command instead of a shell $ xterm -title doughnut # name the window; joyriders' favourite $ xterm -geometry 100x34+60+40 The geometry syntax is COLS×ROWS+X+Y — columns first, then pixels for the corner. It reads odd the first three times and obvious forever after. Note: xterm -e goes away with the shell inside it — close htop, window closes. For a window that survives the command, use -hold (see the hero vocabulary, section 12) to watch errors at the end of scripts that flash by too fast. 03 The three mouse menus xterm's “settings UI” never made it into a GUI box; it is three pop-up menus wired to Control chords while the pointer is over the window. No one would design this today; everyone who has learned it refuses to give it back. Chord Menu What lives there Ctrl + Left-click Main Options Log to File, Print, Secure Keyboard (screen grab), Interrupt / Terminate / Kill, Continue / Suspend, Signal SIGQUIT — the emergency room. Ctrl + Middle-click VT Options Scrollbar toggle, Jump Scroll, Reverse Video, Auto Wrap, Curses Emulation, Select to Clipboard, Locator — the daily behaviour panel. Ctrl + Right-click VT Fonts Font sizes (Largest to Tiny), Escape (default), ASCII, fonts by name — the fast font dial. Two entries deserve a second sentence: Secure Keyboard grabs input exclusively for this window; other clients (your IME daemon, anything) stop reading the keyboard. Useful for passwords when you want to be sure. Select to Clipboard flips the copy behaviour to fill the modern CLIPBOARD — section 08 explains why that single menu entry ends the ancient “xterm cannot copy” myth. Warn: in the Main Options menu, Interrupt/Terminate/Kill are what their names say. Ctrl-Left-click exists precisely so nobody lands there by habit. 04 Fonts, honestly By default xterm draws with its bitmap font, which is why it looks like a library scan from 1989. The moment you point it at a TrueType face it becomes a modern citizen: $ xterm -fa "Liberation Mono" -fs 12 # or, once, in resources (section 06): XTerm*faceName: Liberation Mono XTerm*faceSize: 12 -fa / faceName: any font your X server knows. Run fc-list to see the list; monospace is a good idea, but xterm will not scold you. -fs / faceSize: point size. Set it once; the font menu then cycles sizes relative to it. Ctrl + Right-click → VT Fonts is the size dial for the session; resources are what survives the dial. UXTerm: the same program pre-wired for Unicode; if your terminal draws ? -boxes for non-ASCII, try the UXTerm street name before debugging anything. My font change worked until I resized — then it went back? Menu changes are session-only; resources are permanent. Anything set through a menu dies at the next reboot, anything in .Xresources is for tomorrow. That rule resolves half of xterm folklore. 05 Colors and the 16 known faces xterm speaks 256 colours: the 16 classic ones (resources color0 through color15 ), the 6×6×6 cube, and 24 greys. Applications using ESC sequences or the xterm-256color terminfo can address all of them. The 16 faces every theme talks about — pure CSS, exactly as they ship by default: 0 black 1 red 2 green 3 yellow 4 blue 5 magenta 6 cyan 7 white 8 brblack 9 brred 10 brgreen 11 bryellow 12 brblue 13 brmagenta 14 brcyan 15 brwhite Redefine any of them in resources, with the base pair thrown in: XTerm*foreground: #eef0f8 XTerm*background: #0d0c17 XTerm*color1: #ff5f5f XTerm*color8: #8a8a8a XTerm*cursorColor: #ffd66b And two parlor tricks for the session, no resources needed: $ printf '\033]11;#101820\007' # repaint the background, live $ printf '\033[0;31mred\033[0m' # see? classic red Note: themes from old Unix seasons still work: the menu entry Reverse Video (Ctrl + Middle-click) flips the pair for five seconds of bluescreen comedy. 06 The resource database This is the heart of hero-land. xterm has no config file of its own; it reads the X resource database. In practice you write them in ~/.Xresources and load: $ xrdb -merge ~/.Xresources Then new xterms inherit. A starter file that combines this page's earlier sections: # ~/.Xresources — xterm block XTerm*loginShell: true XTerm*faceName: Liberation Mono XTerm*faceSize: 12 XTerm*scrollBar: true XTerm*scrollbar*thickness: 12 XTerm*saveLines: 4096 XTerm*scrollKey: true XTerm*foreground: #eef0f8 XTerm*background: #0d0c17 XTerm*cursorColor: #ffd66b XTerm*selectToClipboard: true How to find every button's name without reading the source: $ appres xterm XTerm # full resource dump for the class Note: the hierarchy is Class.instance*resource (or * to skip levels). XTerm*faceName hits all xterms; xterm.debugshell*faceName would hit one named instance only. Wildcards are free; laziness with them is not. Note: some systems ship .Xdefaults plumbing instead; it works the same at X startup day one. The two-file confusion dissolves the moment you standardise on .Xresources + xrdb -merge . 07 Scrollback and the frozen screen The two experiences people actually have with scrollback: history that stops being kept (the buffer was small), and a screen that stops moving (the famous Ctrl+S accident). History that stops dying XTerm*saveLines: 4096 # default is 1024; give back some RAM XTerm*scrollBar: true XTerm*scrollKey: true # any key output scrolls back to the prompt Use it: Shift+PgUp / Shift+PgDn line-wise, Ctrl+PgUp faster (per translations , section 12 for custom chords), or drag the scrollbar you switched on above. The frozen screen sheet If output freezes while you type — and typing still works — that is not xterm dying. Press Ctrl+S out of habit, you paused the pipe: Ctrl+Q # unfreeze (xon) $ stty -ixon # in your shell rc: no Ctrl+S/Q at all, ever Warn: everything else on this page is configuration. This trap is not: the classic “xterm hangs” complaint is usually the flow control that the session inherited and the user did not know was there. 08 Copy-paste without mystery X11 has two buffers, and xterm behaves like the person who insists on the rule rather than the spirit: Buffer Filled by Pasted by Meaning PRIMARY Simply selecting text Middle-click The original X way — selection is the copy. CLIPBOARD Explicit copy actions Ctrl+V in modern apps The other systems' way, arrived in X via the desktops. xterm by default works in PRIMARY : select, middle-click, done. Two bridges to the modern world, pick one: One resource line — the friendly one: # ~/.Xresources — selection also lands in CLIPBOARD XTerm*selectToClipboard: true Custom chord — explicit copy keys, like every modern editor (this uses translations , the same machinery as section 10): XTerm*VT100.translations: #override \n\ Ctrl Shift <Key>C: copy-selection(CLIPBOARD) \n\ Ctrl Shift <Key>V: insert-selection(CLIPBOARD) The Ctrl+Shift chord version is what anyone coming from a modern editor tries first; the resource version is what your muscle memory will thank you for. Doing both is also legal. Note: they left double-click word selection smart ( charClass in the hero vocabulary teaches it what “a word” is in URLs and paths), and triple-click selects the line. That is 90% of daily needs, and nothing installs to provide them. 09 Alt, Meta and other ghost stories xterm predates convention convergence, so it keeps knobs for the two ghosts: one where Alt does not reach your shell's readline (Alt-b goes forward a word in bash, but on some feet it does not), and one where 8-bit bytes arrive where escape sequences were expected. # ~/.Xresources — the two ghost exterminators XTerm*metaSendsEscape: true # Alt-b arrives as ESC b, readline understands XTerm*eightBitInput: false # no raw 8th-bit mode; escape prefixes instead metaSendsEscape is the fix for “Alt chords do nothing in the shell, but do in other terminals”. With it, Alt arrives as the ESC prefix your readline always wanted; it is what most modern emulators hard-code. eightBitInput:false keeps everything inside a 7-bit world of control sequences, where remote shells and TUIs thank you daily. Verify with the shell's own report instead of guessing: stty -a (look for ixon , isig ), and the terminal's own vocabulary: TERM=xterm-256color tput colors . Note: if delete/backward keys argue back (sending ^? or ^H , often depending whether you came through PuTTY, ssh, or your own machine), the resources backarrowKey and deleteIsDEL are the honest dials. On a well-configured stack both end up matching the shell's expectations — test, then set. 10 Titles by escape sequence Programs can rename the window or the icon with simple escape output; xterm accepts it if window operations are allowed for that window. $ printf '\033]2;doughnut shop\007' # rename the window title $ printf '\033]1;icon name\007' # rename the icon title If nothing happened, that is privacy-by-default, not a bug: XTerm*allowWindowOps: true # let escape sequences run window ops XTerm*dynamicColors: true # let them re-paint the palette too And you can test the same contract right here on this page — in JavaScript, no escape sequences required: ↬ hijack this page's title ↵ restore Note: the shell-side habit worth copying: PS1 's \e]2;\W\007 tail keeps the title as current directory, and your window manager lists become a trail of clear breadcrumbs. One line, permanent, revertible by removing the line. 11 The resize ritual Split the screen, drag a pane, and the shell inside still believes the old size — wrapping lines at column 80 in a 200-wide window, or worse: truncating the right half silently on the next long command. This is not xterm's fault; it is the shell's knowledge of the geometry lagging behind: $ resize # tells the shell the true size, right now $ resize -u # else export two stty lines for eval $ eval "$(resize -u)" # the way it is actually used in fish/zsh/rc files Resizing locally, without the helper, uses the shell itself: $ stty rows 34 columns 100 Note: most modern shells catch SIGWINCH and follow along by themselves. When one does not, resize is the five-letter command that ends the conversation. It ships with xterm, which is why this manual keeps insisting you install the package and not some appimage of it. 12 Hero vocabulary The one-time dose: flags and resources that separate “it opens” from “I steer it”: Spell What it does -hold Window survives the -e command; script output sticks around instead of flashing by. -rv / *reverseVideo Start reversed (bg/fg swapped); old soul, new mood. -l / Log to File Session tape recording — training, bug reports, receipts. Secure Keyboard Input grab: whole desktop keyboard belongs to this window (password theatre with a badge). -ti vt220 / -tn xterm-256color Lie about your hardware to old programs (vt series) or name the terminfo key. -cc class[:range,...] Teach double-click what counts as “a word” — URLs, paths, hyphens and all. -xrm "resource: value" One-shot resource override on the command line — perfect for experiments without touching the files. *translations The key-translation table — per-key bindings, per-chord scroll, per-button paste. The section 08 example is your template. *charClass The same word-selection teaching, as a resource (persistent cousin of -cc ). ~/.Xterminator The name you give your .Xresources block when you want to feel like a wizard — loading it stays an xrdb job. Warn: a hero vocabulary does not mean writing resources for every window. Settle the 12 lines of section 06 in .Xresources , add the two chips of section 09, and stop. The machines of people with 300 resource lines are no faster; they are just harder to reproduce on the next laptop. Note: truth scoreboard: all of the above is documented in xterm(1) and xterm-ctlseqs(7) , two documents remarkably grounded comparing to the field. Reading them once beats a forum thread; keeping both in your MANPATH beats ten. 13 Your ladder to hero Progress below is stored in this browser ( localStorage ) only. 0 / 12 RESET Launched xterm with -ls , -e and a custom -geometry Named all three menus from their Control chords, unaided Set faceName + faceSize and used the fonts menu Recolored at least one of the 16 + cursor via resources ~/.Xresources written and merged with xrdb -merge Found a resource by yourself with appres saveLines raised and the scrollbar switched on Hit the Ctrl+S freeze and answered it (Ctrl+Q, stty -ixon ) in the same minute Clipboard bridge chosen: selectToClipboard or the Ctrl+Shift translation pair metaSendsEscape set; Alt-b walks backwards in the shell Renamed a window by escape sequence (and owned the allowWindowOps moment) Fixed a stale shell size with resize after splitting
